Hyundai recalls over 250 Tucson SUVs in SA over airbag safety concerns

Owners of certain Hyundai Tucson vehicles are being urged to act after a national recall was announced over concerns that some models may have been fitted with side-impact airbag sensors that do not meet the required specifications.
The National Consumer Commission (NCC) announced the recall of 253 Hyundai Tucson NX4 vehicles that were made available for sale across South Africa in 2025.
Affected vehicles
According to the commission, the recall follows information from Hyundai Automotive South Africa indicating that some affected vehicles may have been fitted with side-impact airbag sensors with incorrect specifications.
The NCC said vehicle owners should have their vehicles inspected as soon as possible to determine whether the correct sensor has been installed.
“Some vehicles may have been fitted with a side impact airbag sensor with incorrect specifications.”
Read more

Assessment
Consumers who own affected Hyundai Tucson NX4 models are urged to contact their nearest authorised Hyundai dealership and book an inspection.
Hyundai will use its diagnostic (GDS) equipment to determine whether it fitted the correct side-impact airbag sensor during production.
“Owners must have the affected vehicles inspected using Hyundai’s diagnostic (GDS) equipment to determine whether the correct sensor has been fitted.”
Inspection
The commission stressed that the inspection process aims to identify affected vehicles and ensure any necessary corrective action is taken without delay.
Hyundai dealerships nationwide have been instructed to inspect vehicles and carry out any required remedial work if a faulty or incorrect sensor is identified.

“Consumers who own affected vehicles are urged to book an inspection at their nearest authorised Hyundai dealership.”
Cost
The NCC also assured consumers that they will not incur any costs related to the recall process.
“Any remedial work will be carried out at no cost to the consumer.”
The commission encouraged affected motorists to respond promptly to the recall notice and arrange inspections to ensure their vehicles meet the required safety specifications.

news_title: More than 50 vehicle recalls in SA this year, but where are the Chinese brands? - EWN
efet_title: More than 50 vehicle recalls in SA this year, but where are the Chinese brands? - EWN
efet_body:
South Africa has been swamped with vehicle safety recalls, with more than 50 instances recorded just this year.
These usually affect legacy brands - established big names like Volkswagen, Toyota and Ford, for instance.
But, considering the influx of Chinese models which now make up more than 19% of our new vehicle sales, why are these largely absent from the list?
As Wendy Knowler points out, just one Chinese-owned brand appears in the recall notices issued by the National Consumer Commission (NCC) in 2026.
But, according to NCC records, the problem with the driver's seat of the MG3 - produced by SAIC Motor in China - emerged during Euro NCAP testing.
As consumers, the way we are alerted to recalls is through the NCC, which has strict guidelines requiring carmakers to notify the regulator in writing.
A common misconception is that a recall indicates something wrong with a brand, when in fact it shows our checks and balances are working for the consumer.
"It doesn't necessarily mean that the legacy brands are more problematic than the Chinese brands. Recalls are normal in all markets; they're not a scandalous thing. It's actually the sign of consumer protection working as it should."
RELATED:
NCC recalls 291 Volkswagen Amaroks over curtain airbag defect
What you need to know about Isuzu's massive recall of D-Max bakkies
Toyota and Lexus recall: NCC flags safety defect in 6,500 vehicles
Digging a little deeper to find the reasons for the absence of Chinese carmakers in local notices, Knowler found that some brands aren't reporting their recalls to the NCC as they do in other markets.
She cites the example of Chery, one of the biggest Chinese players in the South African market.
The NCC confirmed to Knowler that Chery has effectively been running what they call "silent recalls", including a brake recall on close to 3,500 Tiggo 8 Pro Maxes sold here.
What Chery did was to
send recall notices to their dealers
throughout South Africa on 25 June of a 'brake hose recall campaign': "It told dealers to treat this as a priority because of its impact on vehicle safety and to contact all affected customers and to check unsold stock before handing it over to a buyer."
The Commission didn't know about this at the time, and told Knowler they are investigating.
"When Chery answered me, 1 294 had been repaired, which leaves 2 180 of them on our roads with a brake pipe that could come off its clip and end up too close to the exhaust housing."
"Chery said they did inform the NCC about the campaign on 1 July and heard nothing back despite following up. But the Commission told me they didn't receive the alert. And that email was not a recall notification; it was a request for a product recall form and for guidance on the process."
The Commission is saying that doesn't count as notification.
Knowler's advice is to always check for yourself when you buy a car.
"Maybe you do an internet search and you see that there's been a recall in the UK or in Australia or Europe. The first thing you should do is go on to that brand's website in South Africa, where they'll have a link to something like recalls or problems, where you'll find the list of affected VIN numbers."
"I think what the story has told us is: Don't assume because certain brands aren't announcing recalls like the legacy ones, that their cars are all perfect because that would be wrong."
For more detail, listen to the conversation with the consumer ninja in the interview audio at the top of the article
